title: Anthony the Abbot (17 January)
hook: the desert father who heard one Gospel line and walked out; patron of animals, blessed in villages on his day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilary of Poitiers, who chose exile over putting his name to a fellow bishop's condemnation. Your line was hilary the steady. Did you get a chance to say your one true sentence? Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

Two graves are fresh in an Egyptian village, and the young man who buried them was their son. He has land, a younger sister to look after, and a lot on his mind. One day he walks into church while the Gospel is being read, and the line being read, his biographer says, landed on him as if it had been read for him alone. He walked out of that church and started giving his fields away. In some villages, on his feast in January, people still bring cows, horses, dogs and chickens to be blessed in his name. Today, the man from the desert, and how a farmyard ended up on his day.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN, NEWLY ORPHANED.` → `ONE GOSPEL LINE.` → `HE GIVES HIS FIELDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Anthony's story comes to us through the Life of Antony, written by Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria we met yesterday. The line Anthony heard was Jesus speaking to the rich young man in Matthew's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor". Anthony did it. He kept a little back for his sister, Athanasius says, until he heard another Gospel line, about not being anxious for tomorrow, and gave that away too. He placed his sister with a community of faithful women, and went out to live alone. First at the edge of his village, then among old tombs, then deep in the desert, inside an abandoned fort. He stayed there a long time. Athanasius describes the struggle as a real fight: temptations, fear, nights when he felt attacked. And then the surprising part. People came looking for him. When he finally walked out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed: he looked neither wasted nor overfed, and his mind was calm. Others moved into the desert near him to live the same way, and he taught them. That's why tradition calls him the father of monks. Now the animals. Athanasius tells a small story: wild beasts kept trampling the little garden Anthony grew. He caught one gently and told them all, in effect, I do you no harm, so do me none, and leave. And they left. In time, Christians came to call on him as a patron of animals and farm creatures. So on his day, a priest with holy water in a village square, and a line of farm animals waiting their turn.
screen: `ONE LINE: GO SELL WHAT THOU HAST.` · `ALONE: TOMBS, THEN AN OLD FORT.` · `PEOPLE FOLLOW HIM INTO THE DESERT.` · `THE ANIMALS AND THE GARDEN.` · then, large: `IF THOU WILT BE PERFECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for an animal. Settle, and breathe. If there's an animal near you, a dog, a cat, a bird at the window, give it your full attention for a while. Notice how it breathes. If there isn't one, bring to mind an animal you've loved, or one you saw today. Then decide one small kindness: fresh water, a walk that's longer than usual, a little food for the birds. If you pray, you can give thanks for that creature. If you don't, just let it be good that it exists. The bell holds the time.
Anthony. The Egyptian abbot who heard one Gospel line, gave his land away, and went to the desert. Others followed, and he became the one tradition calls the father of monks.
Your line: the father of monks. Today, do the small kindness for an animal that you chose, and notice how little it takes. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Anthony the Abbot's memorial in January, and in some places priests bless farm animals and pets on or near his feast.
